steps.say: llama.cpp, compiled to WebAssembly, running in a browser tab. Version four claims up to 2.8 times faster on Chrome.
And no size limit, in a runtime where every instance stops at four gibibytes.
steps.caption: No size limit: GGUF over 4GB, as-is

scenes.headline: wllama v4: llama.cpp in a tab
scenes.sub: Where the speed came from, and how big models fit
scenes.say: I'm Ringo. Two changes explain this release: the kernels the build finally compiles, and the workers that carry the layers.

steps.say: Emscripten's CMake toolchain tells the build it is targeting x86.
So ggml never compiled its wasm kernels. Every quantized matmul ran generic C.
One flag fixes the detection. On its own it was worth about twenty percent.
The jump came from relaxed SIMD dot products on top: four 8-bit dot products where the old path widened every weight to sixteen bits.
steps.term: Relaxed SIMD: faster ops, platform-defined rounding

scenes.title: Placing a model bigger than 4 GiB

heads: One wasm instance: 4 GiB, and the model is bigger
The measure asks for rpc workers
The fit fills from the last device back
The rest stays home, with the embeddings

steps.say: Back on 32-bit memory, one instance holds four gibibytes. A bigger model simply does not fit.
So the load measures the CPU side first. Over 3584 mebibytes, it asks for one worker per three gibibytes and starts again.
steps.term: RPC worker: the same wasm, as a ggml-rpc server

steps.say: With a GPU, its layers are placed first, exactly as many as you asked for.
llama.cpp's own fit then fills each worker until one gibibyte of its four is left.
The rest stays in the main instance, with the token embeddings. A worker can end up empty.
llama.cpp thinks it is talking to another machine over ggml-rpc. The socket is a shared buffer.
Two rings per worker, one each way. One copy in, one copy out, and llama.cpp is unchanged.
The author's numbers, Chrome on an M5 Max, CPU only.
The headline 2.8 is prefill on LFM2.5 1.2B: 73 to 207 tokens a second.
steps.caption: LFM2.5 1.2B prefill: 73 to 207 t/s

steps.say: And the author says plainly that the two changes were never measured apart.

scenes.title: LFM2.5 1.2B on a 2016 Intel, prompt
scenes.say: On an older Intel desktop, in headless Chrome, the doubling holds: 9.10 to 20.80. Native llama.cpp on the same cores did 213.71, roughly ten times more.

scenes.title: Qwen3.5-4B BF16 on Chrome, generation
scenes.say: Hybrid gets a model running, not running fast. Twenty layers on the GPU: two and a half times. All of them: twenty.

scenes.text: Put the whole model on WebGPU when it fits. Hybrid and workers are for when it does not.

llama.cpp in a tab: faster because it compiles its own kernels, bigger because it borrows more instances.
